sections.overview: The sable is a forest marten of northern Eurasia, widespread from the Urals through Siberia to the Pacific. It also occurs in China, Mongolia, North Korea, Kazakhstan and Hokkaido.
sections.identification: Adults have a long, flexible body, short feet and a bushy tail. In broad Russian samples, males measured 32–53 cm from head to body and weighed 1.15–1.85 kg; females measured 30–48 cm and weighed 0.65–1.60 kg. These observed ranges vary geographically, and adult males are usually heavier than females. Winter fur is dense and silky; the summer coat is shorter and coarser. Across populations, fur ranges from sandy brown to nearly black, sometimes with a pale throat patch. The sable resembles the European pine marten, Martes martes, but is usually darker, has a shorter tail relative to its body, and hunts more often on the ground.
sections.habitat: The sable inhabits coniferous taiga and mixed forests on plains and mountains, hunting mainly near the ground. In Hokkaido, tracked animals rested in dense stands with fallen wood and foraged in mature forest where rodents were plentiful.
sections.diet: The sable is an adaptable predator, and its diet shifts with season and local prey. In eastern Hokkaido, voles occurred most often in samples, followed by Siberian chipmunks and wood mice. The same study recorded birds, eggs, insects, fish, amphibians, reptiles and crustaceans; fruits were more frequent in autumn and winter, when plant foods can supplement mammal prey. In Barguzin, sables hunt pikas beneath snow and scavenge carrion. This broad menu may help sables compensate when mammal prey fluctuates.
sections.behavior: Sables are generally solitary, use individual ranges, locate prey by hearing and smell, and mark their surroundings with scent. In storms or during human pursuit, they may hide in dens for days.
sections.reproduction: Mating takes place mainly from mid-June to mid-August, though dates vary by region. In sparse populations, courtship may involve chasing, jumps and low rumbling; males may fight where their ranges overlap. After fertilization, the embryo remains dormant for 7.5–8 months before attaching to the uterine lining; it then develops for about 30–35 days, with births from late March to early May. Litters contain one to seven kits, often about three. Newborns are helpless and blind; they open their eyes around one month, leave the den soon afterward, and are weaned at about seven weeks, when the mother begins providing regurgitated food. Young disperse in August.
sections.ecology: Forest structure shapes shelter and hunting: in Hokkaido, sables rested under dense cover that may reduce exposure to red foxes and wind, then foraged in rodent-rich mature stands. Some tracked home ranges overlapped extensively. Food shortages can enlarge home ranges.
sections.conservation: Demand for sable fur drove severe depletion in parts of Russia by the early twentieth century. In 1914, a survey found only about 20–30 sables across the future Barguzin reserve; established in 1916 with a hunting ban, it enabled the population to recover. An IUCN assessment dated 3 March 2015 and published in 2016 classified the species globally as Least Concern, reflecting its large, widespread population.
